reasons: 1. As an HVAC/plumbing owner: my missed-call text back should say who I am, sorry I missed you, and ask one question they can answer, and stay under 160 plain characters (no emoji, no curly quotes) so it is not split and billed in pieces.

2. Stop: yes, mostly. 'Your missed-call text gets a hundred sixty characters to book the job' names my problem (missed calls) and a stake (the job), and frame 0.8s shows a big 160 on a tape measure. A number I did not know plus my own phone problem is enough for 3 seconds.

3. Send: yes, the caption tells me to send it to whoever answers my phones and it is short enough to forward. Save: yes, the exact text (Hi, this is Sam the plumber. Sorry I missed your call. What do you need fixed, and when works for you?) is in the caption and on a clean card, ready to copy. Follow: yes, 'part one of three' and 'part two turns it on' give me a reason to follow for the next one. Link in bio is vague ('free tools') and would not get a tap on its own.
4. No hype, no fake urgency, no pitch. Sources are named in the voice (ServiceTitan, Twilio). Reads like a person, not slop.
5. Clear to a stranger. 'Curly quotes do it too' may lose some owners who do not know what a curly quote is; the caption covers it, acceptable.
6. Trust: yes. Specific, sourced, modest claims, and it admits the limit is about billing pieces rather than inventing a disaster.

7. Bar: C1 yes (stake is the job, backed by about one in seven calls coming after hours; Twilio billing each split piece is a direct cost). S1 yes ('there's no name and no question in it. There's nothing to answer' is the why). C3/S3 yes (one copyable text, three-part checklist, 'count yours' is a do-this-week action under an hour).

Minor, not a FAIL: the hook stake is implied, not counted. A future cut could put the after-hours share in the first 3 s (e.g. 'One in seven calls come after hours. Your text back gets 160 characters to book that job.') for a harder stop.
